vignette: Mr. Rajesh Sharma is a 79-year-old South Asian male who has experienced significant distress since his combat exposure during the Vietnam War in the late 1960s. Currently divorced and working at a warehouse, Mr. Sharma's life has been marked by recurrent intrusive thoughts and memories of the traumatic events he witnessed. He vividly recalls the intense heat and humidity, the sound of gunfire echoing through the dense jungle, and the sight of comrades falling around him. These images are often triggered when he hears loud noises, such as fireworks or construction sounds near his home. Mr. Sharma's days in the warehouse are filled with subtle reminders that trigger his traumatic memories. The sound of heavy machinery revving up can instantly transport him back to the battlefield, causing a surge of anxiety and hypervigilance. He is constantly on edge, always scanning for signs of danger, even when he is surrounded by familiar faces and routines at work. His co-workers have noticed that he often withdraws from conversations during lunch breaks and seems preoccupied. In addition to his hyperarousal, Mr. Sharma has developed a range of avoidance behaviors. He tries to avoid places and situations that remind him of the war, which includes staying away from large crowds or areas with loud noises. This has led to significant social isolation. His interactions with friends have dwindled over time as he avoids gatherings where music is played loudly or there are fireworks displays. Mr. Sharma had come to believe that his experiences in combat were a sign of his inherent weakness and inability to cope with adversity. He felt immense guilt for surviving when so many others did not, believing that he should have done more to protect his fellow soldiers. This negative appraisal has deeply affected how he views himself and the world around him. His daily routine is a testament to his efforts to avoid triggers and maintain some semblance of normalcy. Mr. Sharma often takes long detours on his way home from work, steering clear of areas with construction or traffic jams that might remind him of the chaos and unpredictability of war. He has also stopped watching news reports about conflicts in other parts of the world, fearing that they might evoke similar feelings of helplessness and fear. Over time, these avoidance strategies have taken a toll on his occupational functioning. His manager has noticed a decline in Mr. Sharma's productivity and attention to detail at work. Tasks that once came easily now seem overwhelming, as he struggles to concentrate amidst the constant internal turmoil. The isolation and hypervigilance have also strained his relationships with co-workers, making it difficult for him to collaborate effectively. What frightened Mr. Sharma most was the fear of losing control in public, particularly at work, where such episodes would be especially embarrassing. He was certain that if he were to break down or panic during a shift, it might cost him his job and further isolate him from social interactions. This fear has become a pervasive presence in his life, driving many of his avoidance behaviors. Finally, after months of enduring these symptoms and noticing their increasing impact on his daily functioning, Mr. Sharma decided that he needed help. He had heard about cognitive-behavioral therapy through a friend and was hopeful that it could provide him with tools to manage his distressing memories and feelings. He was most afraid of being trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance but also held onto the hope that with support, he might find a way to reclaim some peace. Mr. Sharma's journey towards seeking help marks a significant step forward, acknowledging that his experiences during combat continue to affect him deeply. Through therapy, he hopes to address the negative appraisals and learn how to navigate his triggers more effectively, ultimately regaining a sense of control over his life and well-being.
